## "25 March 1750/1" — What It Means and Why It's Anomalous

### Background: Why English records use double-dated years

Before England's calendar reform in 1752, the **legal year began on 25 March** (Lady Day). That created a mismatch: the modern (New Style) year starts 1 January, but the Old Style year didn't tick over until 25 March. For dates falling in between — **1 January through 24 March** — clerks wrote both year numbers to remove ambiguity:

> "6 January **1745/6**" = 1745 by Old Style reckoning, but 1746 by modern reckoning.

The left number is the Old Style year; the right number is the New Style year.

---

### Why 25 March is a special case

Here's the problem with your record: **25 March is the very first day of the new year under the Old Style system.** On that day, both the Old Style year and the New Style year carry the same number — there is no mismatch to resolve.

| Date | Old Style year | New Style year | Double date needed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 24 March 1750 OS | 1750 | **1751** | Yes → write "1750/1" |
| **25 March 1750 OS** | **1750** | **1750** | **No — same year either way** |
| 26 March 1750 OS | 1750 | 1750 | No |

A slash notation on 25 March is therefore **anomalous** — the two years should be identical, so there is no basis for writing "/1."

---

### What to do before recording a year

**Do not automatically take the later year (1751).** Instead:

1. **Check the surrounding register entries.** Look at how the clerk dated the entries immediately before and after this one. Where does the clerk's year number change — does it flip on 25 March, or a few entries earlier or later? That tells you whether the clerk was using Old Style or New Style conventions and whether the "/1" was a simple slip of the pen.

2. **Look at the record form.** Some registers had printed year headings; the clerk may have been straddling a page headed "1750" while writing into what he knew was "almost 1751."

3. **Note the anomaly in your research notes.** Record the date exactly as written — `25 March 1750/1` — and flag that the double-date notation is irregular for this calendar day.

---

### What to record in your research notes

Until you've checked surrounding entries:

> "Marriage recorded as **25 March 1750/1** (English Old Style register). Double-date notation on 25 March is anomalous — OS and NS years are both 1750 on this date. Year requires verification against adjacent entries. Provisionally citing as **25 March 1750**."

If surrounding entries confirm the clerk was already using New Style year numbering (i.e., the year had already changed to 1751 on 1 January), then cite it as **25 March 1751**. If the clerk was strictly Old Style, **25 March 1750** is correct. Either way, add a note explaining which convention you followed and why.
